mendacious

men-DAY-shus · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Mendacious means lying on purpose -- a mendacious person or statement puts forward claims the speaker knows to be false.

Reporters eventually exposed the executive's mendacious claims about the company's safety record.

Example

The senator's mendacious testimony unraveled once investigators produced the very documents he had sworn did not exist.

Testimony that unravels once the sworn-nonexistent documents appear is exactly mendacious.

Your Turn

Answer correctly to continue.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

deceitful: Deceitful means working to create a false impression by any means -- staged evidence, a doctored photo, a disguise, not only words. Mendacious is narrower: it points at the lies themselves, the false claims a person speaks or writes.

untruthful: Untruthful is the mild, measured word for saying something that is not true, even once. Mendacious is stronger and more damning: it brands a person or a statement as deliberately, knowingly false.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

veracious: habitually speaking the truth

Where it sits · how deliberate the deception is

misleading → mendacious → perjurious

misleading vs. mendacious: Misleading can happen by accident, through careless wording; mendacious specifically implies an intentional, knowing lie.

perjurious vs. mendacious: Perjurious narrows the lie to sworn, legal testimony under oath, while mendacious describes intentional dishonesty of any kind, in or out of court.

Build the Word

The pieces

root — mendac: lie, falsehood (Latin (mendax, mendacium))

suffix — -ious: possessing the quality of (Latin)

Put it together: Mendacious comes from Latin mendax ('lying'), from menda ('fault, blemish') + -ious -- literally 'full of falsehood.'

Use the root in a new word: amend: The biography spends a full chapter on the senator's mendacity and lets readers draw their own conclusions.
